text: Thank you, Your Honor, may it please the court, Gary Glassman assistant city attorney for the defendant in this case the city of Daytona Beach. We are here on an appeal from a grant of summary judgment by the circuit court of the Seventh Judicial Circuit. I believe the way that the plaintiff has framed this case is that there are basically two issues. The first one is we're short term rentals permitted in residential zoning districts under what I call the prior land development code. And the answer is, we say no. The second issue is, does the what we call the new land development code, continue to prohibit short term rentals in the single family residential zoning district and we say that it does. And, and I know I said this my brief but I just want to be careful by using terms prior and old or new I'm not conceding in any way that the codes have changed or anything like that, or that the code is somehow subject to this to the statute that's now preempted local ordinances regarding short term rentals. I think there's a key here that needs to be understood about zoning codes and land development codes and we've discussed a little bit it appears in the brief and it appears in the motions. And that is when you when you interpret or interpret when you look at a code zoning code. See the districts single family multifamily whatever the district may be. And then what you do is you have a chart. And the chart tells you what is permitted. But it doesn't tell you what's prohibited, because if they were to do that for every single zoning code designation. The code would be unwieldy because there are so many uses that could be made of a property. It would be just unwieldy so the code tells you what is permitted. And I think that's important to understand because when you look at the prior land development code. What you see that the city specifically designated tourist district for short term rentals, they didn't put it in any other place. I think that it's not even an inference. I think it's very clear that what the city was intending to do was to say, okay, you want short term rentals. Here's the only place that you can do it in the tourist district, and I would cite to the record, Your Honor. It is a quick second. Well, the section that I'm talking about is found on record page 176 where it says this is how you define a code. It's defined by what is permitted, not what is prohibited. And if you look at the section dealing with the tourist development, which is record page 178, you will see that the tourist district T1 talks about accommodations. We know that the code defined accommodations as hotels, motels, tourist court, rooming house, or rental unit intended to be used by transient persons or tourists for overnight or short term lodging. That's the only place in those tourist district, that zoning district. That's the only place that you can have this type of use of the property, not in single family residential properties. I understand that counsel has said, well, they've been doing it for years. Well, I'm sorry that they have. It's our opinion that then they have been violating our code. And, you know, that's probably why the code enforcement department decided to look into these because, in fact, we were learning of the fact that there were violations that were being made of our land development code. So I think it's very clear. I don't think there's any question that the city had in the prior land development code, the prohibition for the commission to only have short term rentals in the tourist development district. To me, it's very clear. Now we go forward and say, okay, the state comes in in 2011 and preempts the issue. But they provided for what I've called a grandfather clause. Grandfather clause essentially says, if you had an ordinance in effect prior to the preemption statute, that can continue to go forward. And in 2015, the city did a word has been repealed. And I'll use that word because that does appear in the ordinance. But I don't think that that word repeal means anything in this particular case. It's just language. You can't have two codes at the same time. So naturally, one has to go and the other has to come in. But by doing that, I don't think the city simply falls into the statute saying that they can't go ahead and continue to prohibit or to permit only having vacation rentals or tourist rentals in the tourist district. In any event, the city after, as was mentioned by council, six years, please understand that in that six years, it was not just this issue that was being addressed by the city. The city created an entirely new land development code for all areas of the code, not just dealing with tourist development or rentals. So the fact that it took them quite a while to do is an enormous task. I can tell you that I don't have it in front of me. But our land development code runs at least 100, 200 pages. And this was an exacting work that was done by the city. So we come forward. And what's clearly there, Your Honor, is the fact that the city wanted to continue and did continue to have the tourist development district as the only place where you could have short term rentals. They continued that. I don't think there was really any change. We talk about accommodation, other accommodations. They were essentially defined the same way. So we have this situation where the city is saying very clearly, we are going to continue to permit short term rentals only in the tourist development district. And to be even clearer about it, they put in the footnote to the code, which says, this is exactly what we are doing. And I know there was a comment about, well, intent is not an exception. But I think when you're looking at a statute and you're trying to interpret it and you're trying to interpret our code, I think the intent of the city was very clear. And what they were doing by putting in that particular footnote was saying, we are going to continue to permit rentals, tourist rentals, short term rentals, only in the tourist district. And I don't think that the city has done anything else to indicate something otherwise. I just I think that the city has done exactly what it needed to do to comply with the preemption statute. We grandfathered in our prior prohibition or permission of only having short term rentals in tourist districts. So I think that the circuit court made the right decision. The court reviewed the record and I think made the correct decision. So if there are questions, I'll be happy to answer them. But I think that, finally, this court, we would ask that this court, of course, affirm the decision of the circuit court.
